result.text: The paper addresses the problem of domain adaptation when the target domain exhibits relaxed label shift—i.e., changes in label marginals possibly alongside changes in class-conditionals—which existing benchmarks and methods do not systematically evaluate, leaving many heuristics vulnerable to degraded performance. Its key insight is that many popular domain-adaptation heuristics fail under substantial label-proportion shifts, but a simple, broadly compatible two-step correction—pseudo-balancing training data each epoch and then adjusting the final classifier using an estimate of the target label distribution—can substantially recover accuracy. The authors introduce RLSbench, a large-scale benchmark of over 500 shift pairs across vision, tabular, and language tasks with varying label proportions, use it to evaluate 13 methods revealing widespread failures, and show that their meta-algorithm improves accuracy by typically 2–10 points under large shifts while minimally affecting performance when proportions do not shift.

Train CARF from sparse interaction signals—binary success, force/torque, tactile—and enforce object-centric consistency via unsupervised ORF-style decomposition, while using amortized NeRF inference for few-view scenes to keep supervision efficient. The policy consumes both the compact latent and task-conditioned affordance slices sampled along candidate action rays, enabling sample-efficient planning and contact-rich manipulation. We hypothesize CARF improves generalization to novel objects and reduces trial-and-error by grounding actions in learned 3D affordance structure.

Its key insight is that optimistic RL frameworks for policy optimization and value iteration can be adapted with appropriate privacy mechanisms to yield private algorithms whose regret degrades modestly: under joint DP privacy incurs only a lower-order additive cost, whereas under the stronger local DP the privacy cost becomes multiplicative. Methodologically, the authors present two general algorithmic frameworks (one based on policy optimization, one on value iteration), instantiate them with noise-addition and privatization mechanisms tailored to JDP and LDP, and provide a unified regret analysis that establishes sublinear regret bounds and highlights the differing privacy-regret trade-offs.

result.text: The paper tackles camouflaged object detection (COD), where objects blend into complex backgrounds causing ambiguous boundaries and overconfident wrong predictions. Its key insight is to reframe COD as a conditional mask-generation problem and use diffusion-based denoising to progressively refine segmentation while naturally producing diverse plausible masks, thereby reducing overconfident point estimates. The method, CamoDiffusion, conditions a diffusion model on the input image and designs specialized network architecture, loss/training strategies, and sampling schemes to boost expressive power and boundary refinement; stochastic sampling yields multiple candidate segmentations and the denoising process sharpens predictions, yielding state-of-the-art results on multiple COD benchmarks (notably COD10K with MAE 0.019).

result.text: The paper tackles continual learning when a stream of tasks can be a mix of similar (transferable) and dissimilar (unrelated) tasks, a setting where prior methods only handle one or the other and either suffer catastrophic forgetting or miss opportunities for transfer. The key insight is to treat each incoming task adaptively: detect whether it is similar to any previous tasks and, if so, selectively transfer relevant knowledge from those tasks, whereas if it is dissimilar prioritize mechanisms that prevent forgetting. The proposed method implements this by automatically detecting task similarity and then applying different update rules within a single network—selective knowledge transfer for similar tasks and forgetting-mitigation strategies for dissimilar ones—allowing both forward and backward transfer as well as retention. Empirical results on mixed-task sequences show the approach improves new-task learning when transfer is possible while still protecting past-task performance when tasks are unrelated.

The key insight is that when the MDP admits a linear representation for both transitions and rewards (a linear MDP), one can design an exploration algorithm whose sample complexity depends only polynomially on the feature dimension and horizon and not on the number of states or actions, whereas if only the optimal Q-function is linear then reward-free learning can require exponentially many samples. Methodologically, the authors construct a provably efficient exploration procedure for linear MDPs that collects a set of representative transitions and uses linear regression-style estimation to guarantee policy construction for any downstream reward, and they complement this with lower-bound constructions establishing exponential hardness under weaker linearity assumptions.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of how to efficiently discover which tasks should be grouped for multi-task learning, since naively training all tasks jointly can hurt performance and exhaustive search over groupings is computationally costly. The key insight is that the degree to which one task’s gradient would affect another task’s loss during joint training provides a fast, informative signal for which tasks benefit from being trained together. The method trains a single multi-task model once, computes cross-task gradient-to-loss influence measures to quantify positive or negative interactions, and uses these influence values to form task groupings without repeated retraining. On the Taskonomy benchmark this approach reduces test loss by 10.0% versus training all tasks jointly while running 11.6× faster than a recent state-of-the-art grouping algorithm.

args.text: We propose a head-adaptive Nyström KV cache that couples bound-guided budget allocation with compensation tokens and a tiny learned updater. Using the Ada-KV loss bound to assign per-head budgets, we keep full caches for retrieval heads identified via FastGen/RazorAttention and, for other heads, maintain a small set of Nyström landmarks selected by persistence-of-importance; evicted tokens are folded into 1–2 compensation slots whose K/V are updated online by a conditional LoRA projector trained with the recursive compression objective. This yields a streaming kernel approximation to attention with explicit post-eviction error control and minimal retraining, targeting 5–10× KV reduction at negligible quality loss. The method is plug-and-play and compatible with FlashAttention-style kernels.

result.text: The paper addresses the underutilization of unchosen experts in Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models, noting that simply activating more experts can degrade output and that different routing strategies produce substantially different, non-synergistic outputs. The key insight is that unchosen experts still contain useful signals and that contrasting outputs from different activation strengths can surface better next-token probabilities without changing model weights. The authors propose Self-Contrast Mixture-of-Experts (SCMoE), a training-free, inference-time method that computes next-token probabilities by contrasting outputs produced under strong versus weak expert activation of the same MoE model, incurring minimal extra latency. Experiments on multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, StrategyQA, MBPP, HumanEval) show consistent reasoning improvements for Mixtral 8x7B—e.g., GSM8K accuracy rising from 61.79 to 66.94—and further gains when combined with self-consistency.

result.text: UniVisPrompt: a single generalist model that executes diverse image tasks by fusing natural-language instructions or exemplar-based visual instructions with sparse, pixel-level domain prompts, producing either transformed images or dense prediction maps in a deterministic one-step pass. We frame tasks via instruction tuning (as in unified instruction interfaces) and extend visual-instruction learning by encoding before–after demonstration pairs into a “difference” embedding, while injecting SVDP-style sparse prompts at high-shift pixels that are optimized per target image at test time to absorb distribution shift with minimal parameters. A GenPercept-like one-step latent adaptor replaces diffusion sampling overhead and routes features to lightweight task decoders, enabling outputs such as segmentation, depth, or restoration/enhancement within the same architecture. We hypothesize this yields a generalist, instruction-following vision system that adapts on-the-fly to novel domains and tasks with strong accuracy–efficiency trade-offs.

args.text: We propose reward-free reinforcement learning under differential privacy in linear (and linear-mixture) MDPs, aiming to conduct a single private exploration phase that supports near-optimal policies for arbitrary downstream rewards. Our algorithm, DP-RFE, drives optimistic coverage in feature space while releasing privatized sufficient statistics—state-action feature covariances and successor-feature estimates—using batched visitation with Gaussian/Laplace mechanisms and median-of-means to control variance. Theoretically, we show an additive privacy cost under joint DP that preserves the non-private d- and H-dependence up to polylog factors, and a near-optimal multiplicative dependence under local DP via episode aggregation and robust estimation, borrowing ideas from private bandits and GP optimization. Empirically, a single DP exploration dataset delivers performance close to non-private RFE across many post-hoc reward queries, demonstrating the practicality of private reward-free exploration.

result.text: The paper tackles the limitation that existing visual tokenizers are specialized for either images or videos, preventing a unified representation that can leverage complementary spatial and temporal information for generative modeling. The key insight is that a transformer-based tokenizer with a spatial–temporal decoupled architecture—combining localized (window) attention for spatial structure and causal attention for temporal dynamics—can jointly encode images and videos and benefit from progressive, cross-modal training. The method trains OmniTokenizer first on fixed-resolution images to learn strong spatial encodings, then jointly on multi-resolution image and video data to acquire temporal modeling, producing compact latent tokens usable by language-model and diffusion-based generators. Empirically, this unified approach achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction metrics across image and video benchmarks (e.g., ImageNet FID 1.11, UCF-101 FVD 42) and improves downstream generative performance when integrated into different synthesis pipelines.

args.text: We propose Constraint-Weighted Noise-Level Scheduling for plug-and-play diffusion inference: learn an instance-adaptive importance distribution over timesteps (or a monotone reparameterization τ=g(t)) that prioritizes noise levels with the highest estimated constraint-to-denoiser influence. At each iteration we cheaply estimate per-timestep influence by differentiating the constraint through a single denoiser call and using a Hutchinson-style proxy for local curvature, then allocate gradient updates and step sizes to high-influence time bands while regularizing to preserve the effective SNR trajectory. This yields faster, more stable convergence for hard constraints by skipping redundant levels and concentrating compute where constraint satisfaction is most responsive. The schedule composes with interval clustering to avoid negative transfer across distant timesteps and fits within the unified separation of training, sampling, and preconditioning choices.

result.text: The paper addresses 3D shape completion from partial range scans, aiming to produce results that are simultaneously realistic, multi-modal, and high-fidelity. The key insight is to treat completion as a conditional generative task using diffusion models and to improve conditioning by injecting spatially-consistent features at multiple scales and by being occupancy-aware when fusing multiple partial inputs. The method, DiffComplete, implements a hierarchical feature aggregation mechanism that injects local and global conditional features into the diffusion denoising process and an occupancy-aware fusion strategy to flexibly combine multiple partial shapes, which together yield state-of-the-art accuracy (e.g., ~40% L1 error reduction) and strong generalization to unseen classes and real scans without retraining.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of combining multiple task-specific fine-tuned models into a single multi-task model without access to the original training data, a process that naive parameter addition often degrades due to task conflicts and correlations. The key insight is that merging weights can be treated as learnable coefficients and optimized unsupervisedly on unlabeled data by minimizing prediction entropy, which serves as a surrogate objective encouraging confident, consistent multi-task predictions. Their method, AdaMerging, learns task-wise or layer-wise merging coefficients via iterative entropy minimization on unlabeled test samples, producing an automatic task-arithmetic scheme that refines how models are combined. Empirically, AdaMerging improves average performance by about 11% over prior task-arithmetic approaches, generalizes better to unseen downstream tasks, and is more robust to test distribution shifts.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of growing memory and computation costs for Transformer language models in online settings where context continually expands, which degrades inference throughput and limits deployment in constrained environments. The key insight is that accumulated attention key/value pairs can be recursively and compactly summarized into a fixed-size compressed memory that preserves the essential information needed for future attention, enabling near-full-context performance with much smaller storage. Methodologically, the authors integrate a lightweight conditional LoRA module into the model’s forward pass to perform compression of key/value pairs during inference without full-model fine-tuning, and they train this recursive compression by reframing it as a single parallelized forward computation. Empirically, their compressed context memory matches full-context performance with roughly 5× less memory and outperforms sliding-window baselines in streaming unlimited-context scenarios.

result.text: To make approximate machine unlearning resilient to benign relearning and lingering poison effects, we propose Forgetting Nullspace Projection (FNP): learn per-layer subspaces that capture the parameter directions most responsible for the forget set’s influence and project all unlearning and any subsequent fine-tuning updates onto their orthogonal complements. We estimate these subspaces by splitting the forget set into homogeneous clusters based on influence/representativeness, then computing randomized-SVD sketches of per-example influence/gradient vectors within each cluster, optionally in a sparsity-optimized parameterization to keep nullspaces low-dimensional. During unlearning, we pair this projection wrapper with knowledge distillation to preserve retained knowledge, and we prove a simple stay-forgotten bound: under L2-bounded future training updates and smoothness, reactivation along the removed subspaces is zero, bounding recovery of forgotten content and poisoned behaviors. Empirically, FNP should prevent benign data from reawakening memorized sequences in LLMs and speed poison/backdoor removal without full retraining, while remaining compatible with certified unlearning schemes.

args.text: HOI-consistent ego-to-robot view translation: train a 3D-conditioned video diffusion model that converts egocentric manipulation clips into exocentric, robot-eye views without paired recordings. Given ego sequences with recovered camera poses and VISOR masks, the pipeline factors out human-hand occlusions via VIDM while preserving grasp intent, reconstructs a coarse 3D scene/trajectory, and re-synthesizes the interaction from a target robot viewpoint using spatiotemporal diffusion conditioned on the 3D proxy. To keep contacts and grasps physically plausible across views, we inject an HOI prior by fine-tuning with single-frame HOI-Swap edits and enforce object-centric cross-view alignment with an AE2-style loss on hand/object crops. The resulting exocentric clips and aligned 3D interaction traces can supervise visuomotor policies and affordance learners, enabling sample-efficient robot imitation from egocentric human videos.

result.text: The paper tackles the challenge of making vision-language models broadly useful by applying instruction tuning—an approach proven in NLP—to the more complex, multimodal setting where diverse visual inputs and tasks complicate generalization. The key insight is that assembling a large, diverse collection of vision-language datasets into a unified instruction-following format and equipping the model with an instruction-aware Query Transformer to extract task-relevant visual features enables much better zero-shot and fine-tuned performance. Methodologically, the authors convert 26 public VL datasets into instruction-tuning examples, train variants of BLIP-2 with the new Query Transformer on a subset of these datasets, and evaluate on 13 held-out sets, showing state-of-the-art zero-shot results and strong downstream fine-tuning gains compared to BLIP-2 and larger contemporaries; they open-source the resulting InstructBLIP models and code.

args.text: We propose Influence-Weighted Grouped Inference for diffusion plug-and-play, treating denoiser evaluations at different noise levels as related tasks whose gradients toward the constraint objective can positively or negatively interact. Online, we estimate each timestep’s gradient-to-loss influence on the constraint and cluster contiguous timesteps by SNR into high-affinity groups, allocating sampling budget and per-group weights to timesteps that most help the constraint. Within each group we stabilize updates by jointly normalizing magnitudes and rotating directions of per-timestep gradients before aggregating them, reducing destructive interference across scales. This adaptive schedule lowers gradient variance and accelerates convergence for conditional generation and inverse problems without retraining the prior.

result.text: The paper addresses performance degradation in unified generalist models caused by interference among diverse tasks and modalities when using shared parameters. Its key insight is that selectively activating sparse, conditional experts—rather than uniformly shared weights—can reduce destructive interference while keeping computation and generalization efficient. They propose Conditional Mixture-of-Experts (Conditional MoEs) with routing strategies at different conditioning levels to trade off training/inference cost and generalization, and integrate these into the Uni-Perceiver architecture so that only relevant experts are activated per input. This Conditional MoE-enhanced Uni-Perceiver achieves state-of-the-art results on multiple downstream tasks with prompt tuning on just 1% of data while preserving zero-shot transfer to new tasks like video-text retrieval and captioning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of ballooning Key-Value (KV) cache size and the resulting memory/time costs when LLMs process very long contexts. The key insight is that individual attention heads consistently attend to a small set of prompt positions and that this head-specific attention pattern can be predicted from a short “observation” window at the end of the prompt. SnapKV leverages this by clustering and selecting the important KV positions per head (without finetuning) and only storing those compressed KV entries during generation, yielding similar accuracy while keeping decoding latency stable and dramatically reducing memory use. Empirically, SnapKV speeds decoding ~3.6×, improves memory efficiency ~8.2× on 16K inputs, scales to ~380K tokens on a single A100 with negligible accuracy loss, and maintains baseline performance across 16 long-context datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles zero-shot robotic manipulation in unstructured environments where robots must handle novel objects and scenarios not seen during training by decomposing tasks into achievable subgoals. The key insight is that pretrained image-editing diffusion models, which have broad visual and semantic knowledge from Internet-scale data, can be finetuned to predict plausible future “subgoal” observations from a current camera view and a language command, and these visual subgoals can guide a separate low-level goal-conditioned policy more effectively than end-to-end language-conditioned controllers. The method, called SuSIE, finetunes InstructPix2Pix on mixed human and robot video data to generate hypothetical next-view images conditioned on instructions, and trains a robot-specific goal-conditioned policy on robot rollouts to realize those generated subgoal images; at runtime the diffusion model proposes intermediate visual goals that the controller tracks sequentially. Empirically, SuSIE leverages large-scale visual pretraining to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the CALVIN benchmark and strong real-world generalization, outperforming baselines that use privileged information or far more compute and data.

result.text: The paper tackles the mismatch between standard image representations (grids for CNNs, sequences for transformers) and the irregular, complex structure of real-world objects by proposing to model images as graphs; this aims to provide a more flexible, relational inductive bias for visual tasks. The key insight is that treating patches as graph nodes and connecting nearest neighbors lets a graph neural network explicitly aggregate and propagate local and non-local structural information among irregularly arranged image parts. Methodologically, ViG splits an image into patches as nodes, builds a nearest-neighbor graph, and stacks Grapher modules (graph convolution for neighborhood aggregation and update) interleaved with FFN modules (two-layer linear transforms for node-wise feature processing) in both isotropic and pyramid variants, and demonstrates improved performance on classification and detection benchmarks.

The paper addresses how to perform contextual (generalized linear) bandit learning when each user's context and reward must remain private to the server under the strong local differential privacy (LDP) model, aiming to match non-private regret. The key insight is that carefully designed stochastic-gradient-based estimators and update mechanisms can both guarantee LDP and retain the statistical efficiency needed for optimal regret, and that SGD's flexibility can be harnessed for generalized linear bandits where theoretical SGD guarantees are underexplored. Concretely, the authors propose LDP mechanisms that privatize per-round gradient information and use an SGD-style estimator for generalized linear models (and an OLS-based variant for linear bandits) to update parameter estimates while maintaining privacy, and they prove these algorithms achieve the same regret bounds as non-private counterparts. Empirical evaluations on simulations and real datasets confirm the methods deliver strong performance under practical (ε, δ) privacy levels.

The paper tackles the high computational cost of Vision Transformers (ViTs) at inference and training time by reducing the number of tokens processed without retraining or with minimal training. The key insight is that many tokens are redundant (e.g., multiple tokens representing parts of the same object or across frames) and can be merged into representative tokens with little accuracy loss, so selectively combining similar tokens yields large speedups. The proposed method, Token Merging (ToMe), uses a lightweight, general matching algorithm to pair and merge similar token embeddings during forward passes (optionally applied during training), thereby cutting token count and compute while preserving information; empirically ToMe doubles throughput for large ViTs on images, videos, and audio with only ~0.2–0.4% accuracy/mAP drops and can also accelerate MAE fine-tuning.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of blurred and imprecise boundary predictions in semantic segmentation caused by conventional convolutional smoothing. Its key insight is to view boundary feature enhancement as an anisotropic diffusion process and to learn a differentiable operator that amplifies inter-class differences rather than relying on standard isotropic convolutions. To implement this, the authors design a Semantic Diffusion Network (SDN) that approximates the diffusion via a parameterized semantic difference convolution followed by a feature fusion module, producing boundary-enhanced features that can be plugged into encoder–decoder segmentation models. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that inserting SDN yields consistent improvements over typical and state-of-the-art baselines while remaining efficient and flexible.

result.text: The paper addresses why and how training a compact student model to mimic a larger teacher’s class probabilities (knowledge distillation) can outperform direct training on labels and how to make distillation more reliable. The key insight is to view distillation as a semiparametric inference problem where the student is the finite-dimensional target, the true Bayes class probabilities are an infinite-dimensional nuisance, and the teacher provides a plug-in nuisance estimate, which lets one analyze the impact of teacher error on student risk using modern semiparametric tools. Methodologically, the authors derive prediction-error guarantees for standard distillation under this framework and propose two practical improvements—cross-fitting to reduce overfitting bias from the teacher, and loss correction to adjust for teacher underfitting—then empirically validate that these enhancements consistently improve student performance on tabular and image benchmarks.

result.text: The paper addresses the high memory cost of KV caching during generative inference with large language models by proposing a plug-and-play way to compress the KV cache without retraining. The key insight is that attention heads exhibit distinct, predictable structures—some focus on local context, some on special tokens, and some attend broadly—so the cache can be adapted per-head to keep only the vectors that matter. The method profiles attention patterns cheaply, then constructs an adaptive KV cache that evicts long-range entries on local-focused heads, drops non-special tokens on special-token-focused heads, and retains full caches for globally attending heads; this profiling-guided FastGen approach reduces GPU memory use substantially while preserving generation quality and requires no expensive fine-tuning.

result.text: We propose Relearning-Robust Unlearning (RRU), a min–max unlearning procedure that anticipates and immunizes against post-unlearning benign fine-tuning that can rekindle forgotten content. RRU identifies a “forget subspace” via influence/Hessian factors on the forget set, projects parameters to its orthogonal complement, and then unrolls K steps of benign fine-tuning on a proxy corpus in an inner loop while training the outer loop to keep forget signals suppressed—augmented with sparsity to reduce capacity for re-encoding. Building on certified unlearning tools, we derive a practical certificate that any future fine-tuning with bounded step size and budget cannot raise membership or verbatim-recall risk for the forget set beyond a target threshold, using inverse-Hessian sensitivity bounds plus a Fisher/representation-norm constraint at the last layer. This yields unlearning that resists “benign relearning” attacks while preserving utility on retained data.

args.text: DiffMerge-k is a data-free, denoising-aided model merging method for combining multiple task-specific fine-tuned models into a single multi-task model. We learn per-layer, sparse merging coefficients with a differentiable k-selection gate while minimizing unlabeled prediction entropy as in task-arithmetic, but first pass each model’s intermediate features/logits through lightweight diffusion denoisers trained on its own features to suppress noise and magnitude mismatch before computing merges and entropy/consistency losses. We anneal k and add inter-model KL alignment to encourage consensus and reduce destructive interference, enabling robust merging under task correlation and distribution shift without labeled data. We expect sizable gains over entropy-only merging with improved stability, and ablate the roles of denoising, sparsity level, and per-layer vs. global coefficients.

We propose Key-Only Caching with On-Demand Value Rehydration: a training-free scheme that stores only keys per head and reconstructs dropped values when needed via a lightweight per-head linear decoder learned online from a short calibration window. Because K and V originate from the same hidden states with different projections, a ridge-regressed map V≈K·M (per head) accurately recovers values for local/special-token heads, while retrieval heads retain full KV. Coupled with head profiling and adaptive budgets, we trigger rehydration only for positions that survive head-wise selection, achieving large memory cuts without sacrificing global recall. This unifies head-aware budgeting with selective token retention and generative value reconstruction to compress caches beyond eviction-only methods while preserving output fidelity.

result.text: This paper addresses the security risk that machine unlearning—designed to remove specific data from trained models—can be abused to implant backdoors, so that the unlearned model misbehaves in the presence of a trigger. The key insight is that selectively removing particular contributed examples (or combining minor upfront poisoning with later unlearning) can shift model decision boundaries in a controlled way, enabling backdoor activation without obvious tampering of the original training set. The authors propose two attack methods: a pure-unlearning attack that achieves a backdoor solely by submitting malicious unlearning requests for a small subset of the attacker’s contributed data, and a hybrid attack that first plants a few poisoned examples with a trigger and then activates the backdoor via unlearning; both optimize attack utility while maintaining stealth. They empirically validate these attacks across multiple unlearning algorithms, model architectures, and datasets, showing that unlearning mechanisms can be exploited to reliably and covertly insert backdoors.

args.text: We study private reward-free exploration in linear MDPs: how to collect a reward-agnostic dataset that enables near-optimal planning for any downstream linear reward while guaranteeing either joint DP over trajectories or local DP per interaction. Our algorithm, DP-RFE-Lin, marries feature-direction traversal that produces well-conditioned covariates with privatized sketches of Gram and cross-moment matrices (trajectory-level Gaussian noise for JDP; per-step randomized mechanisms with debiasing for LDP), and uses adaptive episodic segmentation so only the last episode’s sufficient statistics are privatized; optimism bonuses explicitly account for both statistical and privacy noise. We show reward-free sample complexity preserves the non-private d- and H-dependence up to an additive O(poly(d,H)/ε_priv^2) term under JDP, while under LDP the privacy cost appears as a near-minimax multiplicative factor, matching known private RL/bandit trade-offs. The privatized covariates suffice for post-hoc planning of any linear reward, yielding ε-accurate value estimates with tight privacy–accuracy trade-offs.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of building a single diffusion model that can represent and generate all marginal, conditional, and joint distributions across multiple modalities (e.g., images and text) without training separate task-specific models. The key insight is that all these distributions can be learned uniformly by treating them as noise-prediction tasks on perturbed multi-modal data, where each modality can have its own perturbation level (timestep); by varying which modalities are heavily or lightly noised, the same model implements marginal, conditional, or joint sampling. The method, UniDiffuser, implements this by perturbing every modality, feeding modality-specific timesteps into a single transformer-based denoiser, and predicting the noise for all modalities simultaneously, so that setting appropriate timesteps enables image, text, text-to-image, image-to-text, or joint generation; when scaled to large image–text datasets it produces realistic samples and achieves competitive FID and CLIP scores versus specialized models.

result.text: Cross-Task Selective Denoising Distillation (CSDD) trains each task in a multi-task model to distill from a small, denoised mixture of other tasks chosen per example. We learn a representation-based task distance and per-example affinities to drive a differentiable k-selection gate that picks the most relevant teacher tasks, then pass their logits/features through lightweight diffusion denoisers with temperature/magnitude calibration before distilling via calibrated KL/ranking losses; teachers are cross-fitted and loss-corrected to reduce bias. Built atop cross-task KD with auxiliary ranking, this yields adaptive, noise-robust transfer without harmful conflicts and scales to large task sets. We hypothesize consistent gains on CTR/CVR and broader MTL benchmarks, with ablations on gating, denoising, and semiparametric corrections.

result.text: Step-Adaptive Token Refinement for Diffusion dynamically allocates spatial token compute across denoising timesteps, leveraging the observation that early steps favor coarse, low-frequency structure while late steps refine high-frequency details. We maintain a persistent hierarchical token graph that is aggressively merged and routed through a compact latent-attention core in early steps, then progressively unmerged only in regions with high predicted residual uncertainty, using cached encoder features to cheaply update masks across adjacent steps. A small controller conditions on timestep and cached features to set per-step token budgets and masks, trained with a consistency loss that distills predictions between merged and unmerged passes. This yields large sampling speedups with minimal quality loss by combining time-step specialization, token merging, coarse-to-fine selection, encoder reuse, and latent interfaces.

result.text: The paper addresses the challenge of large memory and computation costs from Key-Value (KV) caches in long-context language model inference and the limitations of prior token-dropping methods that irreversibly lose information. The key insight is that most attention heads attend only to local context while a small subset of "retrieval heads" attend broadly across the entire input, so preserving full histories only for those heads can retain necessary global information. Building on this, RazorAttention is a training-free compression algorithm that keeps a full KV cache for retrieval heads, prunes remote tokens for non-retrieval heads, and introduces a lightweight "compensation token" mechanism to recover information from dropped tokens. Evaluations on multiple large models show over 70% KV cache reduction with negligible performance loss, and the method is compatible with FlashAttention for efficient, plug-and-play deployment without retraining.

args.text: Gated Expert Quarantine (GEQ) is a MoE-specific unlearning method that localizes and hardens forgetting in the router. We estimate each expert’s contribution to the forget set via per-token routing logs and influence/Hessian factors at expert blocks, quarantine the top-k implicated experts with sparse anti-adapters, and learn a routing mask that zeros their activation on forget prompts while preserving capacity elsewhere; unlearning is paired with retained-data distillation and a negative teacher on forget prompts. We then lock the router with spectral-norm and differential-privacy noise constraints and provide a stay-forgotten guarantee: under ℓ2-bounded post-unlearning fine-tuning, expected activation of quarantined experts and logits for forbidden sequences cannot increase beyond a small epsilon, blocking benign relearning via router updates while leaving shared experts untouched. We target evaluation on MUSE-style LLM unlearning and the benign-relearning pipeline, anticipating higher utility retention than global weight projections and resilience to adaptive deletion sequences via a DP-to-adaptive reduction.

args.text: Robotize-Ego converts human egocentric manipulation videos into robot-compatible visual demonstrations by replacing the human hand with a specified robot end-effector while preserving physically plausible hand–object interactions. We train a conditional video diffusion model that (i) uses VISOR masks and EPIC Fields geometry to factor hand/object and enforce 3D contact/pose consistency, (ii) leverages VIDM-style inpainting to recover occluded scene content, and (iii) adopts HOI-Swap priors to adapt grasps to object shape and function. The "robotized" rollouts provide robot-view-consistent subgoal images and sequences that supervise goal-conditioned policies and 3D affordance fields (e.g., CARF/NeRF-RL) without paired human–robot data. We hypothesize this bridging reduces the human–robot domain gap and improves zero-shot generalization across novel objects and manipulators by conditioning on end-effector kinematics and contact geometry.

result.text: The paper addresses the inefficiency and manual effort in diffusion-based image editing (DIE) where semantic masks are typically created offline or by hand, slowing down Text-to-Image editing workflows. The key insight is that cross-modal attention maps produced by pretrained T2I diffusion models already localize edit-relevant regions, so by extracting and refining these attention distributions one can generate instant, accurate masks without extra training. The method, Instant Diffusion Editing (InstDiffEdit), uses a training-free refinement scheme to denoise and adaptively aggregate attention maps across diffusion steps to produce automatic masks that guide localized edits, and the authors validate this approach on ImageNet and Imagen while introducing an Editing-Mask benchmark. Experiments show InstDiffEdit achieves superior image quality and editing fidelity compared to state-of-the-art methods while running 5–6× faster.

args.text: We propose private reward-free exploration in linear MDPs, designing traversal policies that collect sufficient statistics for any downstream reward while guaranteeing joint or local differential privacy. Our method adapts reward-free feature-direction exploration to operate in privacy-preserving episodes: we aggregate only last-episode sufficient statistics with calibrated noise (JDP) and, under LDP, have users privatize per-trajectory feature occupancy and transition sketches, then robustly aggregate via median-of-means. The resulting private covariance control yields well-conditioned design matrices and linear model estimates whose privacy cost enters as a polylogarithmic additive term under JDP and as a near-minimax multiplicative factor under LDP, implying õ(d poly(H))/ε^2 overhead while retaining reward-agnostic optimality guarantees. We further show that these privatized statistics suffice to plan near-optimal policies for arbitrary rewards with the same dependence on d and H as non-private reward-free algorithms, up to the optimal privacy factors.

result.text: We propose Monotone Time Warping for Diffusion MTL: a learned, differentiable reparameterization τ=g(t) of the diffusion timetable that increases local task affinity across denoising steps to reduce negative transfer. We optimize g (a monotone spline) online to maximize a proxy for cooperativity—the sum of cross-timestep gradient-to-loss influences within a small window—while regularizing to preserve the overall SNR distribution, so training reindexes steps without changing the denoiser or noise budget. This plug-in schedule composes with per-timestep routing like DTR and with MTL optimizers, effectively clustering high-affinity steps and stretching conflicting regions. Empirically, it should tighten early low-SNR regions and smooth late-step transitions, improving sample quality and convergence without adding parameters.

result.text: Amodal3D-Diff completes 2D amodal masks by explicitly reconstructing the full 3D object shape from the visible region using a category-agnostic diffusion model, then projecting the completed shape back to the image to obtain the amodal silhouette. Given an RGB image and its visible mask, we lift a partial 3D observation (via monocular depth/normals) and run a 3D diffusion-based completion conditioned on visible-only features, yielding a distribution over plausible full shapes whose projections induce candidate amodal masks. To encode learned shape priors without letting occluders leak in, we guide denoising with a retrievable codebook/expansion-prior memory and subsequently apply a lightweight discrete diffusion refiner in 2D to snap boundaries to image evidence. Sampling provides calibrated uncertainty and supports multi-view/temporal consistency training, improving robustness under heavy occlusion and ambiguous completions.

result.text: Step-Adaptive Token Refinement for Diffusion dynamically allocates spatial token compute across denoising timesteps, leveraging the observation that early steps favor coarse, low-frequency structure while late steps refine high-frequency details. We maintain a persistent hierarchical token graph that is aggressively merged and routed through a compact latent-attention core in early steps, then progressively unmerged only in regions with high predicted residual uncertainty, using cached encoder features to cheaply update masks across adjacent steps. A small controller conditions on timestep and cached features to set per-step token budgets and masks, trained with a consistency loss that distills predictions between merged and unmerged passes. This yields large sampling speedups with minimal quality loss by combining time-step specialization, token merging, coarse-to-fine selection, encoder reuse, and latent interfaces.

args.text: We propose AttnRD, an online rate–distortion KV cache that jointly decides which entries to retain and at what precision, per head and per token, under a global memory budget. At each step, it estimates attention-output sensitivity to perturbations of individual KV entries using cheap query-curvature probes, then solves a knapsack-style dual to allocate mixed-precision bits and selective retention where they yield the largest distortion reduction per byte. To further smooth the memory–quality tradeoff, AttnRD adds a tiny pool of “distillation bits” to reconstruct dropped entries from nearby anchors via a lightweight affine predictor, instead of hard deletions. The allocation leverages a bound linking KV perturbations to attention distortion (extending Ada-KV’s analysis) and warm-starts with predictable head structures to cut overhead, enabling a plug-and-play, training-free deployment that unifies head-aware selection with fine-grained quantization.

The key insight is that deterministic, learned routing is not necessary and that forcing diverse experts to behave consistently via mutual supervision can make randomly activated experts both robust and parameter-efficient. The authors propose THOR, which stochastically activates a random expert per input during training and inference and trains experts with a consistency-regularized loss so each expert learns from ground-truth labels and from other experts as teachers, encouraging aligned predictions across experts. args.text: We propose Proxy-Moment Label-Shift Estimation (PM-LSE): train a classifier jointly with multiple cheap self-supervised probe heads and calibrate, on a small labeled split, the per-class expected probe-score vectors. On unlabeled target data, estimate target label proportions (including an unknown class) by matching the aggregate probe-score moments to a mixture of the calibrated per-class vectors; infeasibility or residual mass beyond the known-class span signals unknown-class proportion. We then use the estimated class proportions to rebalance self-training and combine probe-predicted instance error with confidence for instance-dependent thresholds, yielding robust pseudo-label selection under relaxed/open-set shifts. This leverages the empirical probe–accuracy correlation for identifiability while providing per-example guardrails inspired by instance-dependent thresholding.

result.text: The paper tackles the inefficiency of uniformly allocating heavy computation across high-dimensional data in generative models, which limits scalability for large images and videos. Its key insight is to decouple expensive global computation from data dimensionality by routing information through a compact set of latent tokens that receive most of the self-attention, while data tokens are accessed via cheaper cross-attention, and to exploit recurrence so routing can be refined gradually during iterative generation. The method, Recurrent Interface Networks (RINs), stacks blocks that alternate bottom-up (data→latent) and top-down (latent→data) cross-attention around a latent self-attention core, and applies latent self-conditioning across diffusion timesteps so latents accumulate and refine knowledge over the reverse process. This architecture is domain-agnostic, enables much more efficient and scalable diffusion-based image and video generation (e.g., single-model 1024×1024 images) and achieves state-of-the-art results while using up to an order-of-magnitude less compute than comparable U-Net baselines.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of performing posterior inference for high-dimensional signals x under an independently trained denoising diffusion prior p(x) together with an auxiliary differentiable constraint c(x,y) that encodes task-specific information y. The key insight is that the denoising diffusion model can act as a plug-and-play prior: by differentiating through its fixed denoiser at multiple noise levels, one can evaluate and optimize the fitness of many noisy variants of x, effectively using the diffusion structure as a stochastic, multi-scale regularizer. The method implements approximate inference by iteratively backpropagating gradients of the constraint through the denoiser at each diffusion timestep (and aggregating contributions across noise levels), enabling conditional generation, segmentation, and other tasks without retraining the generative model.

args.text: We propose a hierarchical multi-resolution KV cache that stores recent tokens at full fidelity while maintaining progressively coarser, head-specific summaries of older context, enabling coarse-to-fine attention and on-demand refinement. At decode time, each head first attends to low-cost cluster/segment summaries to route focus, and only promotes fine-grained KV entries for the selected segments, enforcing a fixed per-head budget with dynamic reallocation. Online, summaries are updated using lightweight, head-tailored clustering/sketching rules and a persistence-of-importance signal to decide which tokens to retain, summarize, or promote, yielding reversible token dropping without retraining. This pyramid unifies per-head behavior modeling, adaptive budgeting, and hierarchical merging to achieve large memory savings with stable latency and minimal quality loss.

result.text: Robotize-Ego converts human egocentric manipulation videos into robot-compatible visual demonstrations by replacing the human hand with a specified robot end-effector while preserving physically plausible hand–object interactions. We train a conditional video diffusion model that (i) uses VISOR masks and EPIC Fields geometry to factor hand/object and enforce 3D contact/pose consistency, (ii) leverages VIDM-style inpainting to recover occluded scene content, and (iii) adopts HOI-Swap priors to adapt grasps to object shape and function. The "robotized" rollouts provide robot-view-consistent subgoal images and sequences that supervise goal-conditioned policies and 3D affordance fields (e.g., CARF/NeRF-RL) without paired human–robot data. We hypothesize this bridging reduces the human–robot domain gap and improves zero-shot generalization across novel objects and manipulators by conditioning on end-effector kinematics and contact geometry.

result.text: The paper addresses how requiring ε-global differential privacy affects regret in multi-armed bandits, deriving tight minimax and problem-dependent lower bounds that reveal two regimes: a high-privacy (small ε) regime where privacy and partial feedback jointly increase hardness, and a low-privacy (large ε) regime where private bandits are no harder than non-private ones. The key insight is that carefully designed, arm-adaptive privacy mechanisms can isolate privacy-induced noise to recent data and thus avoid inflating regret beyond the lower bounds, allowing private algorithms to match non-private performance once ε is large enough and to attain optimal dependence on ε in the privacy-sensitive regime. Methodologically, they prove lower bounds for stochastic and linear bandits, then provide a general recipe to convert index-based optimistic algorithms into ε-global DP versions using the Laplace mechanism, arm-dependent adaptive episodes, and computing private statistics solely from the last episode’s rewards; instantiations AdaP-UCB and AdaP-KLUCB realize this framework, with AdaP-KLUCB matching the problem-dependent lower bound up to constants.

The paper addresses the slow inference time of diffusion-based image and multimodal generation models, proposing an alternative to costly distillation techniques. The key insight is that UNet encoder features change minimally across adjacent diffusion time-steps while decoder features vary substantially, so reusing encoder outputs for multiple steps is feasible and allows parallelized decoder execution. Their method intermittently omits encoder computation by caching and reusing prior encoder features across several time-steps, adds a prior noise injection to recover texture detail, and validates the approach on text-to-image, text-to-video, personalized and reference-guided generation. Applied to Stable Diffusion, DeepFloyd-IF and DiT, this strategy speeds sampling by roughly 24–41% without distilled models and preserves high-quality outputs.

result.text: The paper addresses how to improve cross-task transfer learning by selecting and weighting source-task examples to best help a target task. The key insight is to define a representation-based task distance that quantifies how similar source and target tasks are in feature space and to use that distance to assign target-aware weights to source examples so learning focuses on the most relevant data. The method, Target-Aware Weighted Training (TAWT), computes task distances from learned representations, derives per-example weights that minimize that distance, and trains models (demonstrated with BERT on four sequence-tagging NLP tasks) with these weights; TAWT is simple, efficient, needs little tuning, and comes with non-asymptotic theoretical guarantees while also enabling principled choices about source data and fine-tuning.

result.text: Gated Expert Quarantine (GEQ) is a MoE-specific unlearning method that localizes and hardens forgetting in the router. We estimate each expert’s contribution to the forget set via per-token routing logs and influence/Hessian factors at expert blocks, quarantine the top-k implicated experts with sparse anti-adapters, and learn a routing mask that zeros their activation on forget prompts while preserving capacity elsewhere; unlearning is paired with retained-data distillation and a negative teacher on forget prompts. We then lock the router with spectral-norm and differential-privacy noise constraints and provide a stay-forgotten guarantee: under ℓ2-bounded post-unlearning fine-tuning, expected activation of quarantined experts and logits for forbidden sequences cannot increase beyond a small epsilon, blocking benign relearning via router updates while leaving shared experts untouched. We target evaluation on MUSE-style LLM unlearning and the benign-relearning pipeline, anticipating higher utility retention than global weight projections and resilience to adaptive deletion sequences via a DP-to-adaptive reduction.

args.text: I propose KV-Union: a training-free, hierarchical surrogate memory that unifies head-wise KV eviction with a small, shared global summary to preserve information from dropped tokens. Building on head-specific budgeting and selection, we prune distant tokens per head but simultaneously construct a per-layer surrogate KV set via chunk-wise token reduction and iterative merges; non-retrieval heads query this surrogate set for long-range context while retrieval heads keep full KVs. A lightweight on-demand “write-back” step promotes the most-attended surrogate entries into a head’s cache (compensating for pruned tokens) without retraining and remains compatible with FlashAttention-style kernels. This hybrid design targets larger memory cuts at ultra-long inputs with negligible loss by combining adaptive per-head sparsification with HOMER-like hierarchical summaries and RazorAttention-style compensation.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of machine unlearning—efficiently and accurately removing specific training samples to satisfy data-erasure requests (e.g., GDPR) without degrading model performance. Its key insight is that forgetting can be achieved quickly and precisely by targeting layer-level representations, especially the final layer, and combining targeted sample identification with soft-label transfer to preserve decision boundaries. The method first uses a Partial-PGD algorithm to efficiently locate samples to forget, then performs unlearning confined to the last layer inspired by Forward-Forward, and finally applies knowledge distillation from the original model as a teacher so the updated model retains accuracy via soft labels. Experiments comparing to state-of-the-art unlearning methods show this layer-attack unlearning is both faster and more accurate in end-to-end unlearning performance.

args.text: HIERARCH-KV proposes a streaming, hierarchical, and partially reversible KV-cache compression scheme that assigns per-head, distance-aware budgets via adaptive bounds, preserves sparse full-resolution anchors for retrieval heads as in RazorAttention/SnapKV, and merges the remaining remote tokens within segments using HOMER-style hierarchical chunking to produce a small set of summary KVs. Each segment stores a tiny side-code that enables just-in-time refinement: when a query’s attention to a compacted segment spikes, the method reconstructs the top-k original KVs inside that segment on the fly, while keeping steady decoding latency in the common case. To enable practical deployment without full finetuning, the summary and residual projections are realized with lightweight conditional adapters trained in the single-forward compressed-memory framing, yielding a compact, model-attached compressor that works across layers. This hybrid yields near-full-context accuracy with 5–10× memory reduction in unlimited-context streaming, while maintaining logarithmic peak memory and strong plug-and-play compatibility.

result.text: The paper tackles the efficiency-accuracy tradeoff in large vision-language models for long-term, dense video streaming, where many vision tokens improve understanding but blow up memory and computation. The key insight is that instead of reducing the number of vision tokens (which can lose cues for LLMs’ contextual key-value caches), one can learn to skip expensive per-layer computation for a large fraction of tokens—i.e., a mixture-of-depths strategy that routes most vision tokens forward unchanged while only a subset receive full transformer processing. Extensive experiments on narration, forecasting, and summarization benchmarks (COIN, Ego4D, Ego-Exo4D) show the approach yields state-of-the-art efficiency and accuracy tradeoffs in video-language streaming.

The key insight is that DiT inference exhibits three kinds of redundancy—spatial (many heads attend locally), temporal (neighboring timesteps produce similar attention outputs), and conditional (conditional and unconditional passes are similar)—which can be exploited post-training to avoid repeated costly attention computations. result.text: The paper tackles the gap between diffusion models and multi-task learning by explicitly designing architectures that route task-specific information across the denoising timesteps. args.text: We propose Influence-Matched Co-Training for plug-and-play–friendly unified multimodal diffusion. During training of a UniDiffuser-style model, we interleave standard denoising with episodes that inject lightweight proxy constraints c(x,y) and backpropagate their losses through the denoiser across timesteps and modalities to estimate per-(m,t) gradient-to-loss influence; we then cluster contiguous (m,t) bands and apply DTR-style routing plus within-group gradient normalization/rotation, while meta-learning a small policy that predicts per-(m,t) weights from y. At test time, the same policy drives grouped gradient aggregation in plug-and-play inference, aligning with the model’s trained sensitivity profile to reduce destructive interference and the number of iterations. AmodalSync3D-Track reconstructs temporally consistent per-object 3D shapes for video amodal instance segmentation and tracking by running a single synchronized conditional diffusion over a window of frames and canonicalized object viewpoints, coupling intermediate denoising states across time and views to enforce correspondence. result.text: We propose Influence-Matched Co-Training for plug-and-play–friendly unified multimodal diffusion. During training of a UniDiffuser-style model, we interleave standard denoising with episodes that inject lightweight proxy constraints c(x,y) and backpropagate their losses through the denoiser across timesteps and modalities to estimate per-(m,t) gradient-to-loss influence; we then cluster contiguous (m,t) bands and apply DTR-style routing plus within-group gradient normalization/rotation, while meta-learning a small policy that predicts per-(m,t) weights from y. At test time, the same policy drives grouped gradient aggregation in plug-and-play inference, aligning with the model’s trained sensitivity profile to reduce destructive interference and the number of iterations. result.text: The paper tackles the problem of evaluating approximate machine-unlearning methods for large language models, where exact retraining to remove specific private or copyrighted training data is infeasible. Its key insight is that prior evaluations are too narrow, so unlearning should be judged across six concrete dimensions—no verbatim memorization, no knowledge memorization, no privacy leakage, preserved utility on retained data, scalability to large removal sets, and sustainability under sequential removals—to reflect both data-owner and deployer concerns. The authors introduce MUSE, a benchmark that operationalizes these six criteria and uses them to assess eight popular unlearning algorithms on 7B-parameter models tasked with forgetting Harry Potter books and news articles. Their experiments show that while many methods reduce verbatim and knowledge memorization to varying extents, most suffer from privacy leakage, utility degradation, poor scalability, or inability to handle successive removal requests, highlighting practical limitations and guiding future work.

result.text: The paper addresses how to perform knowledge distillation when the teacher is a decision-based black box that only returns hard labels and when training data may be unavailable, a realistic setting due to storage or privacy constraints. The key insight is that a sample’s distances to the teacher’s decision boundaries capture its relative robustness to other classes and can be used to synthesize soft labels for KD even when only class decisions are accessible. Methodologically, when data are available they compute boundary-distance-based soft labels for each training example and train the student with standard KD; when data are absent they generate pseudo-samples optimized to be maximally distinguished by the teacher’s boundaries, assign soft labels via the same distance-to-boundary scheme, and use these synthesized pairs as the transfer set to train the student.

The paper tackles the problem of ballooning Key-Value (KV) cache size and the resulting memory/time costs when LLMs process very long contexts. The key insight is that individual attention heads consistently attend to a small set of prompt positions and that this head-specific attention pattern can be predicted from a short “observation” window at the end of the prompt. SnapKV leverages this by clustering and selecting the important KV positions per head (without finetuning) and only storing those compressed KV entries during generation, yielding similar accuracy while keeping decoding latency stable and dramatically reducing memory use. Empirically, SnapKV speeds decoding ~3.6×, improves memory efficiency ~8.2× on 16K inputs, scales to ~380K tokens on a single A100 with negligible accuracy loss, and maintains baseline performance across 16 long-context datasets.

result.text: The paper tackles the problem of representation gap in knowledge distillation, where student models produce noisier features than teachers, harming transfer of knowledge across tasks and architectures. The key insight is that many complex KD strategies essentially aim to discard noise and retain valuable feature information, so explicitly denoising student features before matching them to teacher features should improve distillation. result.text: The paper addresses how to better compose and transfer knowledge from fine-tuned pre-trained models by exploiting structure within task vectors (the weight differences from pre-training) to improve multi-task composition, few-shot learning, and robustness to domain shift. The key insight is that parameter blocks of task vectors can be linearly combined with learned, block-specific coefficients to produce anisotropic scaling—only a few coefficients are needed because pre-trained models have low intrinsic dimensionality—so composition can be made more disentangled and less interfering. The proposed method, aTLAS, learns blockwise linear combination weights that scale task-vector components anisotropically, enabling selective mixing of the most informative parameter blocks across tasks and reducing data and memory requirements; experiments show it improves task arithmetic, few-shot recognition, and test-time adaptation under supervised and unsupervised objectives and scales as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning approach.

result.text: The paper addresses the problem of producing non-vacuous, practical generalization guarantees for overparameterized models (especially deep nets) when labeled holdout data is scarce or repeatedly reused. The key insight is that adding fresh unlabeled examples with random labels and comparing model performance on clean versus noisy-labeled data reveals whether the model has truly learned signal: low error on clean data paired with high error on randomly labeled data implies a tight upper bound on true risk. Methodologically, they augment the training set with randomly labeled fresh examples, train as usual, and derive a theoretical bound that is valid for 0-1 ERM and linear models trained by gradient descent—leveraging the early learning phenomenon in deep networks—to yield empirically tight, non-vacuous guarantees on vision and NLP tasks under a mild intuitive assumption.

result.text: The paper addresses how to perform imitation learning when expert demonstrations come from a different MDP than the learner’s environment—differences can include dynamics, viewpoint, or morphology—so direct state-action matching is impossible. The key insight is that one can learn a cross-domain correspondence using only unpaired, unaligned state-only trajectories by imposing cycle-consistency both in state spaces and in a shared, domain-agnostic latent space, together with a temporal-position consistency constraint to align progression through trajectories. The method trains encoders and decoders for each domain into/from the shared latent space with cycle-consistency losses, and a normalized position estimator to enforce temporal alignment, then maps expert trajectories into the learner’s domain and uses the transferred demonstrations for imitation learning. Experimental results across varied challenging domain pairs show this correspondence and transfer enables effective cross-domain imitation.

The paper examines how to best repurpose large text-to-image diffusion models for dense visual perception tasks and identifies which design choices most affect transfer efficiency and performance. The key insight is that high-quality fine-tuning data and image-level (task-specific) supervision matter more than preserving the diffusion model’s multi-step stochastic sampling—indeed, the stochasticity slightly harms deterministic perception—and that a one-step deterministic adaptation can yield faster, better results. Based on this, the authors propose GenPercept, a deterministic one-step fine-tuning paradigm that adapts diffusion priors in latent space while incorporating task-level image supervision and customizable decoders and losses to recover fine-grained details. They validate GenPercept across multiple dense tasks (depth, normals, segmentation, matting), showing faster inference and improved or competitive performance compared with prior multi-step diffusion fine-tuning approaches.

result.text: We propose Laplacian-Coupled Timestep Adapters (LCTA) for diffusion MTL: attach tiny per-timestep low-rank adapters to a shared denoiser and couple them with a graph-Laplacian penalty whose edge weights are online cross-timestep gradient-to-loss influences, promoting smooth sharing among high-affinity neighbors while decoupling conflicting steps. The influence-weighted graph is updated during training, yielding a soft, adaptive sharing pattern that generalizes hard interval clustering and preserves capacity where interference is high. We compose LCTA with DTR-style channel routing in the backbone and apply joint magnitude–direction gradient alignment within shared layers to further stabilize mixed updates, adding minimal parameters and overhead. This reduces negative transfer across widely separated noise levels and accelerates convergence at fixed compute.
